courseTitle: Continuous Integration & Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) for DevOps

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real open-source project on GitHub (or your own repo) and map its actual workflow to the 6 SDLC stages (plan, code, build, test, release, deploy/operate) exactly as the lesson mapped Northbridge Retail's "save for later" button. Find a real merged pull request, trace what actually triggered its CI, and write one sentence per stage describing the real evidence you found for that stage in that repo.
slots.deliverable: A written 6-stage SDLC breakdown of one real GitHub pull request from an existing project, with one sentence naming the real evidence (commit, Actions run, release tag) for each of the 6 stages.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same repository from the last session, pull up 10 of its real merged commits/PRs and classify the project's actual practice (CI, Continuous Delivery, or Continuous Deployment) based on real evidence, not the README's claims. Then estimate the 4 DORA metrics from real timestamps in its history: time from commit to merge as a lead-time proxy, how many releases happened in the window you looked at as deployment frequency, and whether any merge was quickly followed by a revert or hotfix as a change-failure-rate proxy.
slots.deliverable: A one-page write-up classifying a real repository's practice as CI, Continuous Delivery, or Continuous Deployment with supporting evidence, plus your own rough estimate of its 4 DORA metrics computed from real commit/release timestamps.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a new public GitHub repository with a tiny app (even a one-file Node or Python "hello world" with one test). Write your own .github/workflows/ci.yml modeled exactly on storefront's first workflow from the lesson — checkout, setup-node or setup-python, install, run test — push it, and watch it actually run in the real Actions tab.
slots.deliverable: A real GitHub repository with a working .github/workflows/ci.yml that has run at least once in the Actions tab with a green checkmark.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend your repo's workflow's on: block to combine push (branches: [main], paths-ignore for *.md), pull_request, a workflow_dispatch with one real input, and a schedule cron. Trigger it 3 different ways for real: push a code change, push a docs-only change and confirm it's skipped, and click "Run workflow" manually with your input filled in.
slots.deliverable: A workflow with a combined on: block (push with paths-ignore, pull_request, workflow_dispatch with an input, schedule), with run links proving each of the 3 manual trigger behaviors actually happened as expected.

slots.practicalActivity: Split your workflow into two real jobs — lint and test — with test using needs: lint. Push a change that deliberately fails lint and confirm in the real Actions UI that the test job is skipped entirely. Then fix the lint failure, push again, and confirm both jobs run to completion.
slots.deliverable: A workflow with 2 jobs linked by needs:, plus two real Actions run links — one showing the downstream job skipped after an upstream failure, one showing both jobs succeeding after the fix.

slots.practicalActivity: In your repo's Settings, add a real repository secret (any throwaway token-like string) and a repository variable (e.g. a region name). Add a step to your workflow that references both via ${{ secrets.NAME }} and ${{ vars.NAME }}, and confirm in the run log that the secret value is masked as *** while the variable's real value prints.
slots.deliverable: A workflow step using both a real repository secret and a real repository variable, with a run log showing the secret masked as *** and the variable's actual value printed.

slots.practicalActivity: Add actions/cache for your dependency directory keyed on your lockfile's hash, and run the workflow twice to confirm the second run shows a cache hit and installs noticeably faster. Separately, add a step producing a real file (a test report or coverage output), upload it with actions/upload-artifact, and download the resulting zip from the run's summary page.
slots.deliverable: Two real workflow run logs showing a cache miss then a cache hit for the same dependency cache, plus a downloaded artifact zip from a run's summary page.

slots.practicalActivity: Add strategy.matrix to your test job running against at least 2 different runtime versions, and confirm the real run graph shows both running in parallel. Then extract your lint-and-test logic into a separate reusable workflow file declaring workflow_call, and call it from your main workflow with uses:.
slots.deliverable: A real Actions run graph showing a matrix fanned out across at least 2 versions, plus a separate reusable workflow file successfully invoked from your main workflow via uses:.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending GitHub Actions lab: build one consolidated workflow for your repo combining everything from this chapter — a combined on: trigger, at least 2 jobs linked with needs:, a secret and a variable referenced correctly, dependency caching, an uploaded artifact, and a matrix build across at least 2 versions. Run it for real and fix anything that fails until every job is green end to end.
slots.deliverable: One complete, green GitHub Actions workflow run in your own repository exercising triggers, job dependencies, secrets/variables, caching, artifacts, and a matrix build together in a single pipeline.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free Azure DevOps organization and create a new project. Explore the 5 real services (Boards, Repos, Pipelines, Test Plans, Artifacts) in the left navigation, and push or import a small repo of your own into Azure Repos.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure DevOps project with your own small repository pushed into Azure Repos, and a screenshot of the project's service navigation.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real azure-pipelines.yml for your pushed repo with a trigger, a pool, and a BuildAndTest job that checks out code, installs dependencies, and runs your test suite as script steps, modeled on the lesson's storefront-api example. Run it for real in Azure Pipelines and read its run summary.
slots.deliverable: A working azure-pipelines.yml that has run successfully at least once in your Azure DevOps project, with a screenshot of its run summary.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend your azure-pipelines.yml into multi-stage YAML with a Build stage and a DeployStaging stage linked by dependsOn, using a deployment job targeting a real environment you create in Pipelines -> Environments (the deploy step can just echo a message if you have no real target). Add a DeployProduction stage depending on DeployStaging.
slots.deliverable: A multi-stage azure-pipelines.yml with Build -> DeployStaging -> DeployProduction stages chained by dependsOn, run successfully against 2 real environments you created in your Azure DevOps project.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real variable group in Pipelines -> Library with at least 2 variables (one marked secret), and reference it in your pipeline with variables: - group:. If you have any real external account to connect (even a free-tier cloud account), create one real service connection and reference it by name in a pipeline step.
slots.deliverable: A real variable group in your Azure DevOps Library referenced successfully by your pipeline, with at least one secret-marked variable confirmed masked in a run log.

slots.practicalActivity: In Azure Boards, create 2 real work items and a kanban board. Open a real pull request against your repo's main branch referencing one work item's ID in the PR description, and add a branch policy on main requiring your pipeline's build job to pass before the PR is allowed to merge.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Boards work item automatically linked to a pull request, plus a branch policy on main that blocks merging until your pipeline's build job succeeds, demonstrated with one real blocked-then-unblocked PR.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real unit test suite (even 3-5 simple tests) to your repo if you don't have one yet, and add a test step to your GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines workflow that runs it with --maxfail=1 (pytest) or the equivalent fail-fast flag. Push a commit that deliberately breaks one test and confirm the pipeline fails and shows red on the commit; fix it and confirm green.
slots.deliverable: Two real pipeline run links from the same repo — one showing a red failed status check from a broken test, one showing green after the fix — both visible on the commit or PR.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real linter (ruff, eslint, or your language's equivalent) to your repo and a lint step to your pipeline as its own job, separate from test. Push code with a deliberate lint violation and confirm the lint job fails independently of the test job. If using GitHub, also enable CodeQL code scanning on your repo and let it run once for real.
slots.deliverable: A pipeline with lint as its own named job, shown failing independently of a passing test job on one real run, plus one real CodeQL code scanning run visible on your repository's Security tab.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a coverage tool to your test step (pytest-cov, jest --coverage, or the equivalent) with a real --cov-fail-under (or equivalent) threshold like 80%. Confirm the pipeline passes above the threshold, then comment out enough tests to drop below it and confirm the pipeline now fails specifically on the coverage gate, not a broken test.
slots.deliverable: Two real pipeline runs from the same repo proving the coverage quality gate works both ways — passing above your chosen threshold and failing (specifically on the coverage check, not a test failure) below it.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real multi-stage Dockerfile for your repo's app (a builder stage plus a slim runtime stage, exactly like the lesson's storefront-api example). Build it locally first to confirm it works, then add a build-image job to your pipeline guarded by needs: [test, lint] so it only runs after both succeed, tagging the image with the real triggering commit's SHA.
slots.deliverable: A working multi-stage Dockerfile and a pipeline job that only runs after test and lint succeed, producing a real container image tagged with the triggering commit's SHA.

slots.practicalActivity: Push your built image to a real registry (GitHub Container Registry via docker/login-action is free and simplest) and confirm it lands in your repository's Packages tab. Push a second commit to create a second version, and confirm both versions are listed separately rather than one overwriting the other. Pull the first version back down locally by its exact tag to confirm pinning actually works.
slots.deliverable: At least 2 separately-versioned images in your real GitHub Packages (or other registry), both pullable by their exact commit-SHA tags, with the first version proven to still exist after the second was pushed.

slots.practicalActivity: Create 3 real environments (dev, staging, production) in your GitHub repo's Settings -> Environments or your Azure DevOps project's Pipelines -> Environments. Add a 3-job deploy chain to your pipeline (deploy-dev -> deploy-staging -> deploy-production, each linked with needs:) where each step just echoes which environment it targeted, and run it to confirm the order is enforced.
slots.deliverable: A real pipeline with 3 named environments (dev, staging, production) chained by needs:, with one run confirming production cannot be reached except through staging and dev in order.

slots.practicalActivity: On your real production environment (GitHub or Azure DevOps), configure a required reviewer/approval rule. Trigger your pipeline and confirm the production job actually pauses in a pending state until you (or a second account) click approve, rather than running automatically like staging does.
slots.deliverable: A real pipeline run where the production deployment job visibly paused in a pending/waiting state until a required approval was manually granted, with a screenshot of the approval request and the subsequent successful run.

slots.practicalActivity: If you have a real Kubernetes cluster from an earlier course (minikube/kind is fine), set maxUnavailable/maxSurge on a Deployment and watch kubectl rollout status during an update to see pods replaced gradually. Then write a one-page comparison choosing which of the 3 strategies — rolling, blue-green, canary — you'd use for 3 real scenarios: a routine bug fix, a database schema change, and a risky checkout-flow change, with reasoning for each.
slots.deliverable: Real kubectl rollout status output from a rolling update against your own cluster, plus a written strategy choice with reasoning for 3 named deployment scenarios (or the written comparison alone if no cluster is available).

slots.practicalActivity: Add a simple feature-flag check to a real piece of your app's code — even a basic one reading an environment variable or config file — so the same deployed code behaves two different ways depending on the flag's value. Deploy it once with the flag off and confirm old behavior, then flip the flag's value and confirm the new behavior appears with no new deployment.
slots.deliverable: The same deployed build demonstrated behaving two different ways by flipping one flag/config value, with no new deployment or pipeline run between the two demonstrations.

slots.practicalActivity: If you have a real Kubernetes Deployment running, run kubectl rollout history, then deliberately deploy a broken image tag, confirm it's unhealthy, and run kubectl rollout undo to revert it, watching kubectl rollout status confirm recovery. If no cluster is available, write the exact rollback command sequence and what each command's output would need to show to confirm success.
slots.deliverable: Real kubectl rollout history, rollout undo, and rollout status output showing a deliberately broken deployment successfully rolled back to its previous healthy revision (or the equivalent written, fully-annotated command sequence if no cluster was available).

slots.practicalActivity: Write a small real Terraform config (a single free-tier resource, or a local-only null_resource/local_file to keep cloud cost at zero) with a backend you control. Add a GitHub Actions workflow running fmt -check, init, validate, and plan on every push, confirming the real plan output appears in the run log, exactly as Northbridge Retail's pipeline does in the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A real CI workflow that runs terraform fmt -check, validate, and plan against your own Terraform config, with a run log showing the actual plan output.

slots.practicalActivity: On a real cluster (minikube/kind), add a deploy job to your pipeline that runs kubectl set image (or helm upgrade --install) against a Deployment you control, followed by kubectl rollout status --timeout to block until healthy. Push a change, let the pipeline build a new commit-SHA image tag, and confirm the deploy job actually updates the running pods and waits for them to become healthy before finishing.
slots.deliverable: A real pipeline run that built a new image tag, applied it to a live Kubernetes Deployment with kubectl set image or helm upgrade, and blocked on kubectl rollout status/--wait until the new pods were confirmed healthy.

lessons.title: GitOps With Argo CD or Flux

slots.practicalActivity: Install Argo CD (or Flux) on a real local cluster (minikube/kind) following its quickstart, and create one real Application resource pointing at a Git repo path with syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true. Change something directly in the cluster with kubectl edit on a managed resource and confirm Argo CD detects the drift and reverts it back to match Git automatically.
slots.deliverable: A real Argo CD (or Flux) installation with one synced, Healthy Application, plus proof that a manual kubectl edit change to a managed resource was automatically reverted by selfHeal.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Build a Full CI/CD Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own capstone plan exactly as the lesson describes: define your storefront-api-style service (reuse a real repo from this course if you have one) and write out, step by step, which of the 6 pipeline requirements (trigger, build+test, build+push image, auto-deploy to staging, require approval for production, deploy to Kubernetes) you will build and in what order, including your fallback scoping cuts if you run short on time.
slots.deliverable: A written capstone plan naming your real service/repo and listing all 6 pipeline requirements with an explicit build order and a scoping fallback list if time runs short.

slots.practicalActivity: Execute your kickoff plan for real: build (or extend) a complete pipeline implementing as many of the 6 requirements as you scoped, wiring together your own repo, registry, environments, and (if you built one) Kubernetes cluster from earlier chapters into one working end-to-end workflow file, following the lesson's own worked example as a template.
slots.deliverable: A real, executed CI/CD pipeline in your own repository that builds, tests, builds and pushes a container image, and deploys to at least a staging environment automatically, with a passing run to show for it.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real README for your capstone repository explaining what the service does and what the pipeline does stage by stage, plus the "why" behind your key decisions (why staging got Continuous Deployment but production got Continuous Delivery, if you built that gate). Capture a screenshot of a real green pipeline run and practice narrating your own pipeline stage by stage out loud, as if answering "walk me through what happens when you push a commit" in an interview.
slots.deliverable: A capstone repository with a real README explaining the service, the pipeline stage by stage, and your design decisions, plus a screenshot of a real passing pipeline run.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can design and build a real, working CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines end to end — automated tests, static analysis, and coverage gates; container image builds pushed to a registry; staged promotion through dev, staging, and an approval-gated production; rolling/blue-green/canary rollout strategy choices; feature flags and rollback recovery; and Terraform and GitOps-driven Kubernetes deployment — and has a complete, portfolio-ready pipeline project to show for it.
